Anchored by her celebrated installation Flying Girls (2015–16), I Will Belong to Only Me embodies Alatise’s artistic prowess, conceptual depth, and multidisciplinary command across architecture, painting, sculpture, and storytelling. ABOUT THE ARTIST Peju Alatise (b. 1975, Lagos) is a Nigerian interdisciplinary artist, architect, and author whose practice spans sculpture, installation, painting, film, and fiction. She lives and works between Lagos, Nigeria and Glasgow, UK. Trained in architecture at Ladoke Akintola University of Technology, Alatise began her career balancing architectural work with studio practice. Her art engages themes of gender, power, spirituality, and African identity, often grounded in Yoruba cosmology and narrative traditions. "August Wilson: The Writer’s Landscape" is the first-ever permanent exhibition dedicated to Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright August Wilson, exploring how his Pittsburgh upbringing profoundly shaped his acclaimed American Century Cycle. This 3,600-square-foot exhibit guides visitors through three acts: "The Coffee Shop," inspired by his early observational writing, a replica of "The Office" showcasing his personal items and manuscripts, and "The Street," a recreation of Pittsburgh’s Hill District featuring an interactive map, video, and authentic props and costumes from his Broadway productions. Attendees will gain insight into major themes from his plays and discover the timeless relevance of his artistic legacy.

is an immersive audio installation and listening environment by NYC born artist and composer Hprizm, whose practice spans a wide array of genres, including music, performance and multimedia installations. He is a co-founder of the seminal hip-hop group Antipop Consortium, an experimental collective known for their lyrical approach to electronic music.

Wielding his phone as a primary recording device, the artist took notice of his sonic environment while traversing New York City and western Pennsylvania, where he partially resides. In his own words, “The sound of the city, in a literal sense, is dense. Buried histories rumble beneath the foundation of brick. Crate digging and knowledge of self unearthed a cultural medium that informs my process.”

For Hprizm, sound carries strong implications—not only about personal narrative, but about socioeconomic conditions and resources as well. He writes, “Within the throughline for most of my work is an interrelation between memory and sonic imprints. Over the course of the last few years, with global events in mind, I noticed how much the sonic landscape changed. During the pandemic, the streets were quiet. Then there was the sound of unrest and protest. Things went silent again, and then there was a slow crescendo back to normalcy.”

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily.

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Among the noises heard within the work are soul records that the artist and his father once listened to during long road trips, heavily gated drums echoing off New York City Housing Authority tiles and the mechanical grinds of Eastern Ohio and Western Pennsylvania steel factories, to name only a few. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

Whereas these prior iterations presented a visual component as its centerpiece, Sound of the City isolates and concentrates viewers’ attention on a score. In doing so, the work amplifies our awareness of the ways in which noise shapes memory, identity and perception.

Originally presented at Pioneer Works, Brooklyn, the exhibition will be expanded and adapted for Wood Street Galleries at the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust, where it will incorporate new audio recordings and sculptural works. Leading up to the exhibition, the artist will visit  locations throughout Pittsburgh to capture the distinctive sonic textures of our riverfronts, steel mills, transit corridors, churches, social halls, and city parks. These recordings will be remixed into the evolving composition, tying this presentation of the work intimately with Pittsburgh's cultural rhythms and lived experiences. To extend the exhibition beyond the gallery walls, QR codes will be placed at select recording locations linking to the final audio work transforming the sites into portals for listening.

Fiasco Theater and The Public partner to celebrate a hidden American classic: THE VERGE by Susan Glaspell, Pulitzer Prize winner and founder of the Provincetown Players. In Glaspell’s 1921 masterpiece, botanist Claire Archer is on a quest to create a new life: a plant unlike any that has ever come before. When her husband, lover, and soulmate each arrive in her greenhouse seeking heat in a snowstorm, chaos ensues. But as Claire pushes–sometimes violently—against the constraints of her own good breeding, she wonders if the only way to transcend boundaries is to destroy them. By turns witty farce, devastating philosophical debate, and scathing feminist cry, THE VERGE defies genre and pierces the bounds of theatrical realism.

for a tour presentation of her debut album, The Prophet and the Madman. Ami's commanding, operatic voice carries the record from intimacy to theatrical release.

The partnership between Ami and Washington anchors the project, heard most clearly on "How I Became a Madman," a meditation on the tension between chaos and clarity. Together they build something that feels both rooted in tradition and pointed toward what comes next, connecting North African and Middle Eastern music with the improvisational spirit of contemporary jazz.

Ami's international resume includes performances across Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, and the United States, among them the Dutch Royal Metropole Orchestra, the Hollywood Bowl Jazz Festival, and City Winery Boston. Washington, a Grammy winner and Emmy nominee, remains one of his generation's defining musical voices, moving fluently between jazz, soul, hip hop, classical, and screen work.

This is a chance to experience The Prophet and the Madman as it was meant to be heard, live, with Ami's storytelling and vocal range meeting Washington's musical universe, in our seated concert venue with dinner and wine service part of the night. Doors open at 6:00 PM and 9:30 PM.

Step onto the 50-yard line for the New Hazlett’s first-ever co-production with DEMASKUS Theater Collective:
Othello of the End Zone, or The Steel City Tragedy
. Written by Franky D. Gonzalez, directed by Shaunda Miles McDill, and starring Cynthia Dallas and Michael Patrick Trimm, this high-stakes modern reimagining brings Shakespeare to the Northside stage. When Imani Othello is named Head Coach of America's most beloved football franchise, the pressure mounts on and off the field. This hard-hitting adaptation centers a Black woman calling the plays at the height of her power, confronting ambition, betrayal, and relentless doubt.

Dates:
October 22–24 at 7:30 PM | October 24 at 2:00 PM | October 25 at 3:00 PM

But while that band is still very much alive, it was never enough to satisfy Lewis’ creative drive. Embracing his roots to earn a rare second round of success, a series of solo Country projects have led to two No. 1 Billboard Country Album debuts - TOWN LINE (2011) and SINNER (2016) - plus a PLATINUM collab with heroes George Jones and Charlie Daniels (“Country Boy”), and a GOLD-certified Billboard No. 1 with “Am I The Only One” in 2021. Lewis’ 2022 solo album followed suit, with FRAYED AT BOTH ENDS emerging as the best-selling Country album in America but he never wrote songs for the stats.

is an immersive audio installation and listening environment by NYC born artist and composer Hprizm, whose practice spans a wide array of genres, including music, performance and multimedia installations. He is a co-founder of the seminal hip-hop group Antipop Consortium, an experimental collective known for their lyrical approach to electronic music.

Wielding his phone as a primary recording device, the artist took notice of his sonic environment while traversing New York City and western Pennsylvania, where he partially resides. In his own words, “The sound of the city, in a literal sense, is dense. Buried histories rumble beneath the foundation of brick. Crate digging and knowledge of self unearthed a cultural medium that informs my process.”

For Hprizm, sound carries strong implications—not only about personal narrative, but about socioeconomic conditions and resources as well. He writes, “Within the throughline for most of my work is an interrelation between memory and sonic imprints. Over the course of the last few years, with global events in mind, I noticed how much the sonic landscape changed. During the pandemic, the streets were quiet. Then there was the sound of unrest and protest. Things went silent again, and then there was a slow crescendo back to normalcy.”

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily.

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Among the noises heard within the work are soul records that the artist and his father once listened to during long road trips, heavily gated drums echoing off New York City Housing Authority tiles and the mechanical grinds of Eastern Ohio and Western Pennsylvania steel factories, to name only a few. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

Whereas these prior iterations presented a visual component as its centerpiece, Sound of the City isolates and concentrates viewers’ attention on a score. In doing so, the work amplifies our awareness of the ways in which noise shapes memory, identity and perception.

Originally presented at Pioneer Works, Brooklyn, the exhibition will be expanded and adapted for Wood Street Galleries at the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust, where it will incorporate new audio recordings and sculptural works. Leading up to the exhibition, the artist will visit  locations throughout Pittsburgh to capture the distinctive sonic textures of our riverfronts, steel mills, transit corridors, churches, social halls, and city parks. These recordings will be remixed into the evolving composition, tying this presentation of the work intimately with Pittsburgh's cultural rhythms and lived experiences. To extend the exhibition beyond the gallery walls, QR codes will be placed at select recording locations linking to the final audio work transforming the sites into portals for listening.

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Among the noises heard within the work are soul records that the artist and his father once listened to during long road trips, heavily gated drums echoing off New York City Housing Authority tiles and the mechanical grinds of Eastern Ohio and Western Pennsylvania steel factories, to name only a few. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

Sound of the City

is an immersive audio installation and listening environment by NYC born artist and composer Hprizm, whose practice spans a wide array of genres, including music, performance and multimedia installations. He is a co-founder of the seminal hip-hop group Antipop Consortium, an experimental collective known for their lyrical approach to electronic music.

Centered on a sonic score that moves between abstract noise and melodic interludes, Sound of the City collapses vinyl records, tape loops and granular synthesis with audio footage captured by Hprizm over the past few years. Wielding his phone as a primary recording device, the artist took notice of his sonic environment while traversing New York City and western Pennsylvania, where he partially resides.

Wielding his phone as a primary recording device, the artist took notice of his sonic environment while traversing New York City and western Pennsylvania, where he partially resides. In his own words, “The sound of the city, in a literal sense, is dense. Buried histories rumble beneath the foundation of brick. Crate digging and knowledge of self unearthed a cultural medium that informs my process.”

For Hprizm, sound carries strong implications—not only about personal narrative, but about socioeconomic conditions and resources as well. He writes, “Within the throughline for most of my work is an interrelation between memory and sonic imprints. Over the course of the last few years, with global events in mind, I noticed how much the sonic landscape changed. During the pandemic, the streets were quiet. Then there was the sound of unrest and protest. Things went silent again, and then there was a slow crescendo back to normalcy.”

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily.

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Among the noises heard within the work are soul records that the artist and his father once listened to during long road trips, heavily gated drums echoing off New York City Housing Authority tiles and the mechanical grinds of Eastern Ohio and Western Pennsylvania steel factories, to name only a few. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

Sound of the City

is a meditation on migration and gentrification while also historicizing moments in time that exist auditorily. Among the noises heard within the work are soul records that the artist and his father once listened to during long road trips, heavily gated drums echoing off New York City Housing Authority tiles and the mechanical grinds of Eastern Ohio and Western Pennsylvania steel factories, to name only a few. These components are then processed and reinterpreted through tape loops and Ableton Live, both of which are widely accessible tools that helped liberate musical production from corporate and academic infrastructures.

This work was originally inspired by the curriculum that Hprzim taught at William Paterson University, which encouraged students to document their environment and, in turn, introduce themselves through sound. The coursework tapped into early electronic music—where tape, voice and environment each factored heavily—and later evolved into PRESSUREWAVE, a multimedia work that was first presented as a work-in-progress by ISSUE Project Room (2013) and then more formally by Penn University (2018) and The Kitchen (2019).

Come see how the world could be. Welcome to HADESTOWN, where a song can change your fate. Winner of eight 2019 Tony Awards® including Best Musical and the 2020 Grammy® Award for Best Musical Theater Album, this acclaimed new show by celebrated singersongwriter Anaïs Mitchell and innovative director Rachel Chavkin (Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812) is a love story for today... and always.

HADESTOWN intertwines two mythic tales — that of young dreamers Orpheus and Eurydice, and that of King Hades and his wife Persephone — as it invites you on a hell-raising journey to the underworld and back. Mitchell’s beguiling melodies and Chavkin’s poetic imagination pit industry against nature, doubt against faith, and fear against love.

A public utility commission is the regulatory body that oversees providers of essential services, such as water, gas, electricity, rail, and transportation, among others. In practice, corporate capture has often led to these bodies running cover for private corporations with monopolistic reach. How they behave in the dawning era of data center buildouts is a shadow looming on the horizon. If we reconsidered ‘public utility’ in the broadest manner, what might that phrase suggest? What would it look like if there were such a commission dedicated to all the little problems and solutions of making life more functional, and fruitful?

What would it look like if there were such a commission dedicated to all the little problems and solutions of making life more functional, and fruitful? And what if governance were so shaped that it was our working partner in that realization of our shared reality, down to those minute details? The exhibition “Public Utility Commission” is an attempt to dial that imagination into some clarity. As such, it is a reflection on privatization and fundamental issues of human spirit—like what we owe one another, and the shared responsibilities to those we exist beside—while predatory forces do their best to pollute and diminish the spaces we tenuously hold together. “Public Utility Commission” features the work of a robust roster of artists—internationally, from England, France, Italy, and the Republic of Georgia; regionally, from Lancaster, Morgantown, Philadelphia, and New York City; and many, locally, from Pittsburgh. “Public Utility Commission” is designed and curated by Jacquet Kehm and presented by the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust. Participating Artists: Peter Barbor David Bernabo Julia Betts David L.

What is a Young Artist Production?
The foundation of PMT’s mission is built on arts education, development, mentorship, and providing performance opportunities for young artists. Students at PMT Conservatory receive a truly unique experience to use their training in fully produced productions of their own in which they take on roles as performers and technical theater crew. Whether a student wishes to pursue a career in the arts or another field, Young Artist Productions provide an opportunity for growth and building transferable life skills in our future leaders. Patrons attending Young Artist Productions will be a part of it all as they experience and enjoy the best of our region’s talented youth in professional-quality entertainment!
